title: First introductions
goal: Greet people at any time of day, introduce yourself, say where you're from and what you do, ask someone's name, and say goodbye — in a polite tone that is safe to use with anyone.
bekal: greet people from morning to night
say *I am X* with the pattern AはBです
say what something isn't with *じゃありません*
ask questions by adding か to the end of a sentence
say your country and your job

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — Evening class
dialogs.intro: Two people meet for the first time in a Japanese class. Read the Japanese aloud first, glancing up at the rōmaji above it, and only then look at the meaning.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [こんにちは|Konnichiwa]。
lines.id: Good afternoon.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [こんにちは|Konnichiwa]。[はじめまして|Hajimemashite]。
lines.id: Good afternoon. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [はじめまして|Hajimemashite]。[わたしは|Watashi wa] [アニです|Ani desu]。
lines.id: Nice to meet you. I'm Ani.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [たなかです|Tanaka desu]。[どうぞ|Dōzo] [よろしく|yoroshiku] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。
lines.id: I'm Tanaka. Please treat me kindly.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [こちらこそ|Kochira koso] [よろしく|yoroshiku] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。
lines.id: Likewise, please treat me kindly.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [アニさんは|Ani-san wa] [がくせいですか|gakusei desu ka]。
lines.id: Ani, are you a student?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[がくせいです|gakusei desu]。[たなかさんは|Tanaka-san wa]？
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you, Mr. Tanaka?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [わたしは|Watashi wa] [がくせいじゃありません|gakusei ja arimasen]。[かいしゃいんです|Kaishain desu]。
lines.id: I'm not a student. I'm an office worker.
lines.literal: I — as-for — student — am-not. company-person — am.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: そうですか。[しごとは|Shigoto wa] [たいへんですか|taihen desu ka]。
lines.id: I see. Is the work hard?
lines.literal: so — is — [question]. work — as-for — hard — is — [question]

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [ちょっと|Chotto] [たいへんです|taihen desu]。でも、[おもしろいです|omoshiroi desu]。
lines.id: A little. But it's interesting.
lines.literal: a-little — hard — is. but, interesting — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: いいですね。[じゃあ|Jā]、また [あした|ashita]。
lines.id: That's good. Well then, see you tomorrow.
lines.literal: good — is — isn't-it. well-then, again tomorrow.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [さようなら|Sayōnara]。[きを|Ki o] つけて。
lines.id: Goodbye. Take care.

notes: **はじめまして is not “hello”.** It literally means “for the first time”, and is used **only at a first meeting**. Greeting an old friend with はじめまして sounds as if you've forgotten them. For everyday greetings, use こんにちは.

**よろしくおねがいします has no single translation.** Literally it's “please treat me well”, and it is used far beyond introductions: when handing over a task, when joining a new team, when ending an email. Think of it as “let's make this go well together”. In an introduction it is almost obligatory — to Japanese ears, an introduction without it feels unfinished.
**こちらこそ = “no, *I* should say that”.** It returns a kind word: if the other person says よろしく first, the most natural reply is こちらこそよろしくおねがいします.

**さん is not exactly “Mr./Ms.”, but it's used almost always.** さん goes after other people's names whatever their gender or age. The key rule: **never attach it to your own name**. Calling yourself “たなかさんです” sounds like you're flattering yourself.

**そうですか with a falling tone = “oh, I see”.** With a rising tone it becomes “oh, really?”. The tone makes the difference, not the words. It's one of the most frequent phrases in Japanese conversation — a kind of “uh-huh” that shows you're still listening.
**でも = but, at the start of a sentence.** Notice that でも begins a new sentence; it doesn't join two clauses mid-sentence the way English “but” often does.

grammars.title: Core pattern: A [は|wa] B [です|desu]
body: This is the first and most important pattern in Japanese: **topic + [は|wa] + comment + [です|desu]**.
**[は|wa]** here is read *wa*, not *ha*. This is the one big exception in reading hiragana, and you'll meet it in almost every sentence.

**[は|wa] marks the topic**, not the subject. The most honest translation is “as for …”: [わたしはアニです|watashi wa Ani desu] = “as for me, Ani”. The difference will matter later, when one sentence has both a topic and a subject.
**[です|desu] means “is/am/are”**, and also signals politeness. It goes at the **end** of the sentence — in Japanese, the verb always comes last.
Pronunciation: [です|desu] is said *dess*, not *de-su*. The final u is barely audible.

head: Topic (は)
Comment
です
Meaning
rows: Mr. Tanaka is an office worker.

after: **The topic can be dropped.** Once it's clear who you're talking about, [わたしは|watashi wa] disappears: [がくせいです|gakusei desu] already means “I'm a student”. Japanese speakers drop it far more often than beginners expect — sentences that keep starting with [わたしは|watashi wa] sound like a textbook translation.

grammars.title: Asking: just add [か|ka]
body: Japanese **does not change the word order** to ask a question, and doesn't need a question mark. Just attach **[か|ka]** to the end.
[がくせいです|gakusei desu] = “You are a student.” → [がくせいですか|gakusei desu ka] = “Are you a student?”

Since [か|ka] already marks the question, ？ is actually redundant. Formal writing ends questions with a plain 。. The ？ is still used in text messages and casual speech — usually precisely when the [か|ka] has been dropped.

head: Statement
Question
Meaning
rows: [にほんじんですか|Nihonjin desu ka]
[たなかさんですか|Tanaka-san desu ka]

after: **Answering:** [はい|hai] (yes) or [いいえ|iie] (no). Politeness doesn't stop there — after [はい|hai] the sentence is usually repeated: [はい|hai]、[がくせいです|gakusei desu].

grammars.title: Saying “not”: [じゃありません|ja arimasen]
body: The opposite of [です|desu] is **[じゃありません|ja arimasen]**. It sits in exactly the same place: at the end of the sentence.
[わたしはがくせいです|watashi wa gakusei desu] → [わたしはがくせいじゃありません|watashi wa gakusei ja arimasen].
There are three forms with the same meaning; they differ only in formality:

head: Form
Feel
Where it's used
rows: Polite everyday conversation. Use this one.

after: **Before you ask:** [じゃ|ja] is really a contraction of [では|dewa] said quickly. Spoken Japanese is full of contractions like this, and the contraction is almost always what you'll hear in real life.

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — At the front desk
dialogs.intro: Ani is signing up at a language school. Notice that the receptionist uses more refined forms than in the first dialogue — note おなまえ, not なまえ.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [いらっしゃいませ|Irasshaimase]。
lines.id: Welcome.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]。[にほんごの|Nihongo no] [クラスは|kurasu wa]…
lines.id: Excuse me. About the Japanese class…

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: はい。[おなまえは|Onamae wa]？
lines.id: Yes. Your name?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [アニ・ウィジャヤです|Ani Wijaya desu]。
lines.id: Ani Wijaya.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [アニさんですね|Ani-san desu ne]。[おくには|Okuni wa]？
lines.id: Ms. Ani, then. Which country are you from?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [インドネシアです|Indoneshia desu]。[ジャカルタから|Jakaruta kara] [きました|kimashita]。
lines.id: Indonesia. I came from Jakarta.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [おしごとは|Oshigoto wa] [なんですか|nan desu ka]。
lines.id: What do you do for work?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [エンジニアです|Enjinia desu]。でも、[いまは|ima wa] [がくせいです|gakusei desu]。
lines.id: I'm an engineer. But right now I'm a student.
lines.literal: engineer — am. but, now — as-for — student — am.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: わかりました。[これは|Kore wa] [がっこうの|gakkō no] カードです。
lines.id: Certainly. Here is your school card.
lines.literal: understood. this — as-for — school — 's — card — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ありがとうございます|Arigatō gozaimasu]。
lines.id: Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: うけつけ:
lines.text: [クラスは|Kurasu wa] [あしたからです|ashita kara desu]。[きょうしつは|Kyōshitsu wa] 2かいです。
lines.id: Classes start tomorrow. The classroom is on the 2nd floor.
lines.literal: class — as-for — tomorrow — from — is. classroom — as-for — 2-floor — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: はい、わかりました。[しつれいします|Shitsurei shimasu]。
lines.id: Yes, understood. Excuse me.

notes: **お before a word = politeness lent to the other person.** なまえ = name, おなまえ = your name. The rule is simple: use お for **other people's** things, never for your own. So おなまえは？ to ask, but to answer just なまえはアニです — or, more often, simply アニです.

**A sentence left hanging on purpose.** にほんごのクラスは… stops halfway, and that is **not a mistake**. Trailing off is Japanese politeness: you leave the other person to finish the thought instead of demanding. Beginners often feel they must complete it; Japanese speakers often don't.

**すみません has three meanings at once:** “excuse me” (to get attention), “sorry” (for a small mistake), and “thank you” (when you've put someone out). If you can't decide between this and ありがとう, すみません is rarely wrong.

**ね at the end of a sentence = seeking agreement**, like “right?” or “isn't it?” in English. アニさんですね = “Ms. Ani, right?”. This tiny word softens a sentence noticeably — without ね, a sentence can sound like a data check.

**しつれいします literally means “I commit a rudeness”** and is used when entering or leaving a room, or ending a phone call. This, not さようなら, is what you say at the office — さようなら feels like a long farewell.
**きました = “came”.** This is the past form; you'll learn it fully in Unit 10. For now, memorize ジャカルタからきました as one ready-made introduction phrase.

grammars.title: Nationality and language: ～[じん|jin] and ～[ご|go]
body: Country names are written in katakana (except a few Asian countries that have their own kanji). From the country name, two more words form automatically:
**～[じん|jin] (人)** = a person from that country. **～[ご|go] ([語|go])** = that country's language.
This pattern has almost no exceptions, so one country name gives you three words at once.
after: **One exception to memorize:** English is **not** [イギリスご|igirisugo] but **[えいご|eigo]**. Arabic, too: [アラビアご|arabiago]. Otherwise, the pattern holds.

grammars.title: Question words: [なん|nan] / [だれ|dare] / [どこ|doko]
body: Japanese does not move question words to the front of the sentence the way English does. The question word **sits in the same position** as the answer — just swap in the part you don't know.
[しごとはエンジニアです|shigoto wa enjinia desu] → [しごとは|shigoto wa]**[なん|nan]**[ですか|desu ka]. It doesn't move an inch.

head: Question word
Meaning
Example sentence
rows: [おしごとは|Oshigoto wa] [なんですか|nan desu ka]. — What do you do for work?
[あのひとは|Ano hito wa] [だれですか|dare desu ka]. — Who is that person?
[トイレは|Toire wa] [どこですか|doko desu ka]. — Where is the restroom?
[おくには|Okuni wa] [どちらですか|dochira desu ka]. — Which country are you from?

after: **[なん|nan] or [なに|nani]?** Both are written 何. Use **[なん|nan]** before [です|desu] and before t/d/n sounds ([なんですか|nan desu ka], [なんじ|nanji]). Use **[なに|nani]** elsewhere ([なにを|nani o] [たべますか|tabemasu ka]). If you get it wrong you'll still be understood — your ear will correct it over time.

⚠️ **Questions with a question word aren't answered with [はい|hai]/[いいえ|iie].** Answering [おしごとはなんですか|oshigoto wa nan desu ka] with [はい|hai] makes no sense — just as “Yes” makes no sense as an answer to “What do you do?”

blocks.text: Japanese greetings are tied to the time of day, and the boundaries are stricter than in English. Saying おはようございます in the late afternoon sounds odd, not just slightly off.

head: Greeting
When
Notes
rows: To close friends, just おはよう. At work it's also used as the first greeting of the day — even if the shift starts in the evening.
The safest greeting when in doubt.
Used when parting at night, not when meeting.
Feels heavy — used when you won't meet for a long time. For everyday partings, じゃあまた or またあした is far more natural.
Literally “you must be tired”. The all-purpose office greeting: when passing in the hallway, when leaving, when closing a meeting.

blocks.text: **Bowing (おじぎ).** Japanese greetings almost always come with a small bow. Rule of thumb: the deeper the bow, the greater the politeness. A 15° nod for everyday greetings, 30° for thanks and formal introductions, 45° for a sincere apology. Keep your back straight and pause briefly at the lowest point — a hurried bow reads as insincere.

sections.title: Names, order, and forms of address

blocks.text: Japanese people say the **family name first**, then the given name: たなか ゆうこ = family Tanaka, given name Yuko. And in everyday life it's the **family name** that's used — たなかさん, not ゆうこさん. Calling someone by their given name signals a closeness that may not exist yet.

head: Suffix
Used for
Notes
rows: Safe for anyone, regardless of gender or age. When in doubt, use this.
Replaces さん, not combined: たなかせんせい, not たなかせんせいさん.
Used for juniors or equals, not for superiors.
Used with someone you've just met, it sounds condescending.
Very respectful. You'll hear it often in shops: おきゃくさま.

blocks.title: Your name in katakana
items: Foreign names are written in katakana, adapted to Japanese syllables: **Budi → ブディ**, **Sari → サリ**, **John → ジョン**, **Emma → エマ**, **Michael → マイケル**, **Lisa → リサ**.
A consonant standing alone gets a u (or an o after t/d): Mark → マー**ク**, Robert → ロバー**ト**.
If your name is long, Japanese people will usually use just part of it — that's not rudeness, just their way of making your name pronounceable.

blocks.text: A self-introduction (**じこしょうかい**) has a set structure in Japan, and people really use it — on the first day at work, in class, at meetings. These lines are all you need:

head: Step
Sentence
Meaning
rows: [どうぞ|Dōzo] [よろしく|yoroshiku] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。

blocks.title: A complete example
items: [はじめまして|Hajimemashite]。[わたしは|Watashi wa] [ブディです|Budi desu]。[インドネシアの|Indoneshia no] [バンドンから|Bandon kara] [きました|kimashita]。[しごとは|Shigoto wa] [エンジニアです|enjinia desu]。[どうぞ|Dōzo] [よろしく|yoroshiku] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。
Nice to meet you. I'm Budi. I come from Bandung, Indonesia. I work as an engineer. Please treat me kindly.
Say it aloud five times with your own name. This is the sentence you'll use most in your first month.
